subject: business-studies
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What is meant by organic (internal) growth?
options: A business grows by using its own resources, such as opening new stores or launching new products
A business grows by buying a controlling interest in another business
A business grows by merging with a competitor of similar size
A business grows by relocating its production overseas
questions.explain: Organic growth is internal expansion funded from the business's own resources, unlike external growth through mergers or takeovers.

questions.q: What is a multinational company (MNC)?
options: A business that produces goods in more than one country and has operations in more than one country
A business owned by shareholders on the stock exchange
A business that only exports goods to other countries
A business that has taken over a foreign competitor
questions.explain: A multinational company has production and operations located in more than one country.

questions.q: How do economies of scale benefit a business as it grows?
options: Average unit costs fall as the level of output increases
Total costs fall as output increases
Selling prices rise as output increases
Fixed costs rise in line with output
questions.explain: Economies of scale mean the cost of producing each unit falls as output rises, improving competitiveness.

questions.q: A government imposes a tariff on imported goods. What is the most likely effect?
options: Imported goods become more expensive, making domestic goods more competitive
Imported goods become cheaper for domestic consumers
Exports from the country automatically increase
Domestic businesses pay higher taxes on their sales
questions.explain: A tariff is a tax on imports that raises their price, helping protect domestic producers from foreign competition.

questions.q: The marketing mix is made up of which four elements?
options: Product, Price, Place and Promotion
Product, Profit, People and Promotion
Price, Place, People and Process
Product, Price, Profit and Place
questions.explain: The marketing mix consists of the four Ps: Product, Price, Place and Promotion.

questions.q: The design mix balances which three elements of a product?
options: Function, aesthetics and economic manufacture (cost)
Function, branding and price
Aesthetics, promotion and place
Quality, cost and packaging
questions.explain: The design mix balances how well a product works (function), how it looks (aesthetics) and the cost of making it (economic manufacture).

questions.q: Why might a business use an extension strategy?
options: To prolong the maturity stage of a product's life cycle and delay decline
To launch a completely new product into the market
To reduce the price of a product during its introduction stage
To remove a product from the market quickly
questions.explain: Extension strategies aim to extend a product's life and delay the decline stage, for example through new packaging or new markets.

questions.q: A firm launches an innovative smartwatch with advanced features no rival has, setting a high initial price to target early adopters. Which pricing strategy is this?
options: Price skimming
Penetration pricing
Loss leader pricing
Competitive pricing
questions.explain: Price skimming sets a high initial price for a new, innovative product to maximise revenue from customers willing to pay a premium.

questions.q: Which production process is used to make one-off, unique products such as a bespoke wedding cake?
options: Job production
Batch production
Flow production
Mass production
questions.explain: Job production makes single, often customised, items one at a time to a specific order.

questions.q: What is a key benefit of using a just-in-time (JIT) approach to managing stock?
options: It reduces the costs of holding and storing stock
It guarantees the business never runs out of stock
It removes the need to work with suppliers
It increases the amount of buffer stock held
questions.explain: JIT delivers stock only as it is needed, cutting storage and warehousing costs but relying heavily on reliable suppliers.

questions.q: How does quality assurance differ from quality control?
options: Quality assurance builds quality checks into every stage of production, while quality control inspects the finished product
Quality assurance inspects finished goods, while quality control prevents errors during production
Quality assurance only applies to services, while quality control only applies to goods
Quality assurance is carried out by customers, while quality control is done by suppliers
questions.explain: Quality assurance is a preventative approach checking quality throughout production, whereas quality control checks the product at the end.

questions.q: A bakery makes 500 loaves of white bread, then switches equipment to make 500 loaves of wholemeal, then 500 seeded loaves. Which production method is being used?
options: Batch production
Job production
Flow production
Cell production
questions.explain: Batch production makes groups (batches) of identical products before switching to make a different batch.

questions.q: How is gross profit calculated?
options: Revenue minus cost of sales
Revenue minus all expenses and interest
Cost of sales minus revenue
Net profit minus operating expenses
questions.explain: Gross profit is revenue less the cost of sales (the direct cost of the goods sold).

questions.q: What is the correct formula for the gross profit margin?
options: (Gross profit ÷ revenue) × 100
(Gross profit ÷ cost of sales) × 100
(Net profit ÷ revenue) × 100
(Revenue ÷ gross profit) × 100
questions.explain: Gross profit margin expresses gross profit as a percentage of revenue: (gross profit ÷ revenue) × 100.

questions.q: A business has revenue of £200,000 and net profit of £40,000. What is its net profit margin?
questions.explain: Net profit margin = (net profit ÷ revenue) × 100 = (40,000 ÷ 200,000) × 100 = 20%.

questions.q: What does the average rate of return (ARR) measure?
options: The average annual profit of an investment as a percentage of its cost
The total revenue an investment generates each year
The time taken to pay back the cost of an investment
The interest a business pays on a bank loan
questions.explain: ARR compares the average yearly profit from an investment to its initial cost, expressed as a percentage.

questions.q: What is meant by the span of control in an organisational structure?
options: The number of employees a manager is directly responsible for
The number of layers of management in a business
The path down which decisions are passed to staff
The process of passing authority to subordinates
questions.explain: Span of control refers to how many subordinates report directly to a manager.

questions.q: What is a typical feature of a flat organisational structure?
options: Few layers of management and a wide span of control
Many layers of management and a narrow span of control
A long chain of command with little delegation
Highly centralised decision-making at the top
questions.explain: Flat structures have fewer management layers, so each manager oversees more staff, giving a wide span of control.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of internal recruitment?
options: Promoting an existing employee to fill a vacancy
Advertising the post in a national newspaper
Using a recruitment agency to find candidates
Hiring a graduate straight from university
questions.explain: Internal recruitment fills a vacancy with someone who already works for the business, such as through promotion.

questions.q: A car dealership pays its sales staff extra money for each vehicle they sell, on top of their basic pay. Which method of motivation is this?
options: Commission
Fringe benefits
Job rotation
Job enrichment
questions.explain: Commission is a financial reward paid according to the amount an employee sells, encouraging higher sales.
